Just reproduced it in a self-contained folder.  Created a `.eslintrc` file with my pasted content above and a `file.js` with the pasted content above and then ran `eslint -c .eslintrc file.js` in that folder and still got that error.

Ah, that is interesting. So this seems to be directly related to using `-c .eslintrc`, which is unnecessary. If you just do `eslint file.js`, it behaves as expected (it automatically pulls in the `.eslintrc` file).

It appears that this is a bug with reading the file specified by `-c`, because if I turn off loading of `.eslintrc` then I get the same issue:

```
eslint --no-eslintrc -c .eslintrc file.js
```

It looks like for some reason the environment in the `-c`ed config file is taking precedence over the rules contained within it, which is definitely a bug.

body: I think you're looking in the wrong spot,`reset` doesn't matter for this issue. The key is that you're trying to change a rule to a different value than what the environment specifies.

My point was that adding a similar test to the ones already in the suite won't help to detect this bug. When `reset: true` is set, as is the case for all tests, there is no default env. config that could mess up with the rules you're trying to change.

I'm sorry, I'm not explaining things very well (serves me right for trying to respond on my phone). The code block you included is the correct area of concern. Is there a reason you can't add a new rule that leaves `reset` as false?

> Is there a reason you can't add a new rule that leaves reset as false?

Mmm, what do you mean by "a new rule that leaves `reset` as false"? Do you mean a new test case calling `Config` with `reset: false`?
Oops yes, autocorrect snagged that. I meant create a new test.

Well, that was my original question :stuck_out_tongue: Since all the tests use `reset: true`, I didn't want to mess up anything by requiring a bunch of environment rules so I could build the expected value of the test. If that's OK I'll just submit a PR.

However, the fix might not be as simple as switching the order of the two merges in the code snippet above. Even if we do that, there is another corner case where we would get something not very natural to me:
- `rootdir/.eslintrc`
  
  ``` yaml
  env:
      node: true
  rules:
      no-mixed-required: 0
  ```
- `someconfig.yml`
  
  ```
  env:
      node: true
  rules:
      // Other rules
  ```

Again `eslint -c someconfig.yml rootdir/app.js` will show `no-mixed-requires` errors. This is because we do something like:

``` javascript
config = baseConfig
merge(config, envRulesFrom(eslintrcFile.env))
merge(config, eslintrcFile.rules)
// Assuming we swapped the erroneous merge order
merge(config, envRulesFrom(configFile.env))
merge(config, configFile.rules)
```

I think that something more natural would be:

``` javascript
config = baseConfig
envs = {}
merge(envs, eslintrcFile.env)
merge(config, eslintrcFile.rules)
merge(envs, configFile.env)
merge(config, configFile.rules)

merge(config, envRulesFrom(envs))
```

What do you think?

The corner case is actually behaving as expected. The passed-in configuration file takes precedence over the `.eslintrc` file. You can see the full priority list here: http://eslint.org/docs/configuring/. The only issue here is that the rules in the `-c` config file are applies before the environments.

As an aside: `-c` is kind of vestigial at this point. `.eslintrc` files were introduced later in the project's lifecycle and really supersede `-c`. We had to make `-c` highest priority to be backwards compatible.
